region.name: Lithic Card Issuing Program
region.summary: Covers the planning and tracking of the Stencil debit card program, which is issued through Lithic on a Pillar Bank BIN, along with related vendor decisions and partner-bank oversight. This includes program design, the slip to a Q1 2027 launch and its action items, staffing and budget asks, and Pillar status updates. It also includes build-vs-buy and KYC vendor choices, plus access review tracking.

brief.text:
The Lithic Card Issuing Program region covers Stencil's debit card. The card is tied to the Stencil balance and issued through Lithic on a Pillar Bank BIN. The program design includes virtual and physical cards, spend controls, layered fraud rules, and round-up savings. The interchange revenue share with Lithic/Pillar is still under negotiation. The soft launch, originally planned for Q4 2026, slipped to Q1 2027. The reason was to protect investing GA and the Series B raise. As a result, cost assumptions built on the Q4 2026 date are flagged as an open risk, alongside the risk that the card could slip again. The asks to Aleks are to sign the Lithic contract, secure Pillar Bank sponsor approval, and allocate $400k for year one. Staffing across engineering, design, product, and compliance totals roughly 0.5 engineer-quarters. Named risks are regulatory exposure (card programs are regulated), missing fraud capacity, and physical card delivery delays. Action items from the program design review were checked off on Oct 7: the timeline change was communicated to Lithic, contract minimums were checked, and card sequencing was covered at the Pillar QBR. Scheduling the compliance review with Priya Shah's team remains open.

Partner-bank oversight runs through Pillar Bank status updates. As of May 26, the in-flight items were: the ACH pipeline change (Pillar comfortable, cut-over meeting June 4), the investing feature (operational impact review, sign-off expected end of May), the KYC migration from Persona to Alloy (approved), and Lithic card issuing on a Pillar BIN (commercial terms under negotiation, owned by Aleks). Pillar conditions also include a $2,500 daily funding cap per user for the first 90 days of investing. Product conventions apply to this work: PRDs follow a standard structure, carry written Decision lines, and use dated action items. Access review tracking also lives here. Each quarter has its own tracker page with status columns. The changelog shows the first version on 2026-07-08, Lithic added with tier changes on 2026-09-14, and the Q3 review opened on 2026-09-21. Two todos with October deadlines are still open.

Vendor decisions follow a buy-by-default rule for anything non-core. Any build proposal requires a written case through the build-vs-buy framework. The framework says to consider building only if all its conditions hold, including that no vendor solves your specific shape of the problem. Logged buy decisions are Alloy for KYC, Lithic for card issuing, DriveWealth for brokerage, and two notification vendors. Logged build decisions are the ACH pipeline, the auto-savings algorithm, and Postgres-based feature serving. ADR-026 moves KYC from Persona to Alloy, with Persona phased out by Q3. The rationale is that Alloy's orchestration allows swapping providers without rewriting the integration, which matters given uncertain FINRA and investing identity-proofing requirements. The move also saves $120k/year and avoids Persona's growth-penalizing pricing. Persona's UX edge is judged fixable with about two weeks of design and frontend work. Typical questions for this region: when the card launches and why it slipped, what budget and approvals are pending, who owns Lithic terms, the status of the compliance review, why Alloy replaced Persona, and the criteria for building versus buying.

items.title: Decision: Allocate $400k for year one
items.summary: Capital allocation covers the platform fee and per-swipe costs at projected volume.

items.title: Decision: Choose Lithic over Marqeta
items.summary: Author recommends Lithic as the card issuing vendor because of better developer experience, graceful pricing at scale, responsive support, and comparable fraud tooling.
